Daniel’s core move—treating Bell-inequality violation as an artifact of the *nonlinearity* of \(\sin^2(\theta/2)\) under an \(L_2\) notion of angle, and then “fixing” it by switching to an \(L_1\) geometry—slides past what Bell-type results actually constrain. Bell’s theorem is not about whether a response curve is linear in a chosen parameterization; it is about whether **one can reproduce a particular family of joint probability distributions with locality + realism**, given freely chosen measurement settings ([Bell 1964](https://cds.cern.ch/record/111654/files/vol1p195-200_001.pdf)). If Daniel re-labels \(\theta\) so that the correlation looks piecewise linear, that does not by itself create a local hidden-variable model; it just changes coordinates. To genuinely “restore” a local hidden-variable explanation, one must change the *achievable correlations*, i.e., the convex set of behaviors allowed by the theory—not merely the metric used to *describe* them.

The interesting avenue Daniel is gesturing at is real, but it lives one level deeper: Bell/CHSH bounds are tightly linked to the **geometry of the state space and the inner product structure** that quantum theory inherits from Hilbert space. The familiar quantum limit (Tsirelson’s bound) can be derived from the Euclidean geometry of vectors/operators and their inner products ([Tsirelson’s bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsirelson%27s_bound)). If one “moves to an \(L_1\) world” in a physically meaningful way, one is not merely changing \(\pi\); one is implicitly changing the symmetry group of rotations, the structure of measurement settings, and likely the underlying probabilistic theory. In the language of generalized probabilistic theories, that means swapping out the quantum convex set for something else; some alternatives give *stronger-than-quantum* nonlocality, others collapse back to classical locality, but the decisive ingredient is the **state/effect geometry**, not the aesthetic crookedness of \(L_2\) space ([GPT overview](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.2390)).

A smaller but telling point: “triangle wave is pure tone” is false in ordinary Fourier analysis; a triangle wave contains an infinite series of odd harmonics with amplitudes falling as \(1/n^2\). That mistake matters because it mirrors the post’s broader pattern: substituting a geometric metaphor (“piecewise linear trig”) for a dynamical/operational claim (“what spectra/correlations are physically realizable”). If Daniel wants the argument to land, he would need to specify what *operational* changes accompany the \(L_1\) shift—how preparation, measurement, and composition rules change—then check whether those rules indeed generate Bell-satisfying correlations rather than just a re-described version of the same quantum ones.
